intro: Athletes bring coordination, discipline and performance under pressure, but their closest matches are only moderately similar. The closest of the 25 careers below is Gambling Managers, with a 71% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $93,220, which is 40% more than the $66,710 athletes earn.
why_it_works: Competing means training on a schedule, reading opponents and making split-second decisions in front of a crowd. O*NET rates coordination at 3.62 out of 5 for athletes, judgment at 3.25 and social perceptiveness at 3.12. Hospitality management, airline and supervisory roles use the same people and timing skills. Most matches need no extra schooling. The gaps are budgets, people management and systems analysis.
tips: Coaching is not in this list but is a common path; see our page for former coaches.
Facilities Managers earn $106,660, which is 60% more, and many venues hire former athletes.
Food Service Managers earn $69,390, or 4% more, and value leadership under pressure.

faq.q: What jobs can former athletes do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Gambling Managers (71%), gambling services supervisors (68%) and Food Service Managers (68%), based on O*NET 31.0. Flight Attendants are also 68% matched and earn $63,580, which is 5% less than the $66,710 median for athletes and sports competitors.

faq.q: Which careers for former athletes pay more?
faq.a: 13 of the 25 matches pay more. Air Traffic Controllers earn $148,080 (122% more), Facilities Managers $106,660 (60% more) and police and detective supervisors $106,040 (59% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. The first two usually need extra training.

faq.q: Do athletes need a degree to change careers?
faq.a: Not for most matches. 17 of the 25 need no more education than athletes already have, including all of the top 10. In the closest match, 57% of workers have a high school diploma or the equivalent, so experience and contacts count most.

faq.q: What skills should former athletes learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are managing financial resources, managing people, systems analysis and managing materials. Instructing already rates 3 out of 5 for athletes in O*NET, so business and leadership skills are the main steps toward management roles.
